subject: computing
subtitle: Writing modular, reusable code using procedures and functions.

data.targetWord: A named, reusable block of code that can be called from anywhere in a program; it is written once and may be used many times

examples.en-GB: A subroutine called printMenu() can be called whenever the program needs to display the menu, without rewriting the code.

data.targetWord: A subroutine that performs a calculation or operation and returns a value to the code that called it using the RETURN keyword

examples.en-GB: FUNCTION add(a, b) RETURN a + b ENDFUNCTION — calling add(3, 7) returns the value 10 to the caller.

data.targetWord: A subroutine that performs an action but does not return a value to the caller; it is called for its side effects such as displaying output

examples.en-GB: PROCEDURE greet(name) OUTPUT "Hello, " + name ENDPROCEDURE — calling greet("Alice") displays a greeting but sends nothing back.

data.targetWord: A placeholder variable listed in a subroutine's definition that receives the value of the corresponding argument when the subroutine is called

examples.en-GB: In PROCEDURE greet(name), the word 'name' is the parameter — a placeholder that will be filled when the subroutine is called.

data.targetWord: The actual value passed into a subroutine when it is called; it fills in the corresponding parameter inside the subroutine

examples.en-GB: In greet("Alice"), the string "Alice" is the argument — the real value that the parameter 'name' will hold during this call.

data.targetWord: The value sent back from a function to the code that called it, via the RETURN keyword; only functions produce return values, not procedures

examples.en-GB: If add(3, 7) returns 10, the return value is 10 — this value can be stored in a variable or used directly in an expression.

data.targetWord: A variable created inside a subroutine that exists only while that subroutine is executing; it cannot be accessed from outside the subroutine

examples.en-GB: The variable 'area' created inside a calculateArea function is local — it disappears when the function finishes.

data.targetWord: To execute a subroutine by writing its name followed by parentheses and any required arguments; a subroutine only runs when it is called

examples.en-GB: Writing calculateArea(5, 3) in the main program calls the function and passes 5 and 3 as arguments.

data.targetWord: To write the code for a subroutine using PROCEDURE/FUNCTION in pseudocode or the def keyword in Python; defining a subroutine does not execute it

examples.en-GB: def greet(name): print("Hello", name) defines the subroutine but does not run it; it runs only when called.

data.targetWord: An approach to programming that splits a large program into smaller, self-contained subroutines, each handling one specific task

examples.en-GB: A program with separate subroutines for getInput(), processData(), and displayResults() uses modular design.

data.targetWord: The ability to call the same subroutine multiple times from different places in a program, avoiding the need to repeat the same code

examples.en-GB: A validateInput() subroutine written once and called from five different places in the program demonstrates reusability.

data.targetWord: The pseudocode keyword (return in Python) that sends a value back from a function to the caller and immediately ends the function's execution

examples.en-GB: RETURN area sends the computed area value back to the main program and stops the function running any further.

data.targetWord: The pseudocode keyword that marks the end of a function's definition block

examples.en-GB: FUNCTION add(a, b) RETURN a + b ENDFUNCTION — ENDFUNCTION closes the function definition.

data.targetWord: The pseudocode keyword that marks the end of a procedure's definition block

examples.en-GB: PROCEDURE displayMenu() OUTPUT "1. Play" OUTPUT "2. Quit" ENDPROCEDURE — ENDPROCEDURE closes the procedure definition.

data.targetWord: The region of a program where a variable is accessible; local variables have scope limited to the subroutine where they are defined

examples.en-GB: A variable defined inside a function has local scope — it exists only inside that function and is invisible to the rest of the program.

data.targetWord: The parameters and return value of a subroutine that define how the rest of the program interacts with it, without needing to know its internal code

examples.en-GB: The interface of calculateArea(width, height) tells callers: pass two numbers in, get one number back.

data.targetWord: A collection of related subroutines and data grouped together so they can be reused across multiple programs

examples.en-GB: Python's math module contains ready-made functions such as math.sqrt() that programmers can import and call.

data.targetWord: The group of indented statements that form the body of a subroutine, executed when the subroutine is called

examples.en-GB: The indented lines underneath a def statement form the block that executes every time the function is called.

data.targetWord: Hiding the internal details of how a subroutine works so that the caller only needs to know what it does, not how it does it

examples.en-GB: Calling math.sqrt(16) without knowing how square roots are calculated is an example of abstraction.

data.targetWord: Breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems, each of which can be solved by a separate subroutine

examples.en-GB: Decomposition turns a complex quiz program into smaller problems: getQuestion(), checkAnswer(), updateScore().

data.targetWord: Any action a subroutine performs beyond returning a value, such as displaying output, modifying a global variable, or writing to a file

examples.en-GB: A procedure that prints a receipt to the screen has a side effect: it changes what is displayed even though it returns nothing.

data.targetWord: A function that does not return a value; in Python this is equivalent to a procedure defined with def but without a return statement

examples.en-GB: A subroutine defined with def but with no return statement is a void function — it performs actions but sends no value back.

data.targetWord: A constant defined at the top of a program or subroutine with a meaningful name in UPPERCASE, used to avoid magic numbers in the code

examples.en-GB: Using CONSTANT PI = 3.14159 inside a circleArea function makes the code clearer than writing 3.14159 directly.

data.targetWord: The Python keyword used to define a subroutine (both procedures and functions); it is followed by the subroutine name and parameters

examples.en-GB: def add(a, b): return a + b — the keyword def signals that a subroutine called 'add' is being defined.

data.targetWord: The Python keyword that sends a value back from a function to the caller and immediately ends the function's execution

examples.en-GB: return area sends the value of area back to wherever the function was called and stops any remaining code in the function from running.

data.targetWord: A Python error that occurs when code tries to use a variable that has not been defined in the current scope, such as accessing a local variable from outside its subroutine

examples.en-GB: Trying to print a local variable after the function has finished causes a NameError because the variable no longer exists.

data.targetWord: The ease with which a program can be updated, corrected, or extended; subroutines improve maintainability by isolating code in one place

examples.en-GB: Using a subroutine means a bug can be fixed in one place rather than hunting for the same logic repeated across many lines.

data.targetWord: Checking that a subroutine produces the correct output for a given input; subroutines can be tested individually in isolation

examples.en-GB: Testing a calculateTotal() function with known inputs such as 5 and 3 and verifying it returns 8 is independent unit testing.

data.sentence: The key difference between a function and a procedure is that a function ____ a value.
A ____ is the placeholder variable listed in the subroutine definition.
An ____ is the actual value passed to the subroutine when it is called.
Local variables only exist ____ the subroutine where they are defined.
A subroutine must be ____ before it will run; defining it does nothing on its own.
Using subroutines reduces ____ because common code is written once and reused.
The RETURN keyword both sends a value back to the caller and ____ the function immediately.
Local variables can only be accessed ____ the subroutine that created them.
Breaking a large program into smaller subroutines, each handling one task, is called ____ design.
In Python, subroutines (both procedures and functions) are defined using the keyword ____.
A procedure performs an action but does NOT ____ a value.
In pseudocode, the keyword that marks the end of a function definition is ____.
Trying to access a local variable from outside its subroutine causes a ____ in Python.
Hiding the internal details of a subroutine so callers only need to know what it does is called ____.
Breaking a large problem into smaller sub-problems, each solved by a subroutine, is called ____.
A subroutine with no return statement (or only side effects like printing) is sometimes called a ____ function.
Using subroutines makes programs easier to ____ because a bug is fixed in one place, not everywhere.
After a RETURN statement executes inside a function, any remaining code in the function ____ execute.
The ____ of a variable refers to the region of the program where it can be accessed.
Each subroutine can be tested ____ with known inputs, making debugging easier.

data.title: What happens when a program calls a function
data.instruction: Put the steps of a function call in the correct order.
items: The main program reaches the line that calls the function
Execution jumps to the function definition and the arguments fill the parameters
The function body executes line by line
The RETURN statement sends a value back to the caller
Execution returns to the main program at the line after the call
The returned value is used — stored in a variable or used in an expression

data.title: Steps to write a function that calculates the area of a rectangle
data.instruction: Put the steps in the correct order.
items: Choose a meaningful function name, such as rectangleArea
Identify the parameters needed: width and height
Write the function header: FUNCTION rectangleArea(width, height)
Calculate the area inside the function body: area ← width * height
Call the function from the main program and store the result: result ← rectangleArea(5, 3)
